program_overview.title: CCC Junior and Senior Preparation
program_overview.tagline: One season, two tracks, real problem solving: from the first CCC Junior loops to the Senior algorithms that lead toward the Canadian Computing Olympiad.
program_overview.description:
The Canadian Computing Competition (CCC) is run by the Centre for Education in Mathematics and Computing (CEMC) at the University of Waterloo. The 2027 contest for North and South America is on Wednesday, February 17, 2027. It has two levels: Junior, for "any participant with beginner to intermediate programming skills", and Senior, for "any participant with intermediate to advanced programming skills", and CEMC says each participant can choose the best level "regardless of their grade". Each level has 5 questions, the time allowed is 3 hours, and it is scored out of 75. CCC participants may use C, C++, Python 2, Python 3 or Java, and the contest is written in school: participants write online, individually.

This course is a full September-to-February season with two parallel tracks. The Junior track follows the skills CEMC's own question guide describes, from basic loops and conditions, through loops, conditions and counting together, up to the recursion, two-dimensional arrays and efficient algorithms of the hardest Junior question. The Senior track starts where CEMC says the Senior paper starts, with sorting and searching, then moves through careful counting and mathematical reasoning toward the algorithms of the final question, which CEMC calls an IOI level question. Both tracks are taught in Python or C++. For Senior students aiming beyond the CCC we teach C++ properly, because CEMC states that "CCO participants must use C++".

Practice comes from two places: our own original problems written for each topic, and CEMC's free past contests, which CEMC publishes with no registration or fee and which students can also try on CEMC's free CCC Online Grader practice account. We never copy contest problems into our materials; students work them where CEMC publishes them. Students register through their school, not through us. We teach the skills and the contest habits, and we make no promise of scores, distinctions, CCO invitations or admissions.

faqs.question: What is the Canadian Computing Competition?
faqs.answer: The CCC is a programming contest run by CEMC (the Centre for Education in Mathematics and Computing) at the University of Waterloo. It has a Junior and a Senior level. Each has 5 questions, the time allowed is 3 hours, and it is scored out of 75. CEMC says the contest is available in English and French and is written in school, with participants writing online, individually.

faqs.question: When is CCC 2027?
faqs.answer: CEMC lists the 2027 CCC for North and South America on Wednesday, February 17, 2027, and the ordering deadline for schools as Thursday, February 11, 2027. Our season runs from September up to that date, and students who join later get a catch-up plan.

faqs.question: Should my child write CCC Junior or CCC Senior?
faqs.answer: CEMC describes Junior as for "any participant with beginner to intermediate programming skills" and Senior as for "any participant with intermediate to advanced programming skills", and says each participant can choose the best level "regardless of their grade". In the first two weeks we place each student on a track by skill, and we review the choice before the contest.

faqs.question: How do we register for the CCC?
faqs.answer: Through a school, not through us. CEMC says "It is not possible for students to individually register for a contest" and "all students must participate through their school." If a student's school does not take part, CEMC suggests that "students can look for another local school that will allow them to join as a participant". We remind families to check the school's order well before the deadline.

faqs.question: Python or C++ for the CCC?
faqs.answer: CEMC says "CCC participants may use C, C++, Python 2, Python 3, or Java." It also notes that "it may not always be possible to achieve a perfect score with a particular language choice (for example, Python or Java)". Python is a sensible choice for most Junior students. For Senior students aiming at the Canadian Computing Olympiad we teach C++, because CEMC states that "CCO participants must use C++."

faqs.question: Do you use CCC past papers?
faqs.answer: Yes, the way CEMC intends. CEMC publishes its past contests free, with no registration or fee, and students can practise on CEMC's free CCC Online Grader account. We set those contests as practice and review them in class, alongside our own original problems written for each topic. We do not copy CEMC's problems into our materials.

faqs.question: What is the Canadian Computing Olympiad (CCO)?
faqs.answer: CEMC says "Approximately 20 of the top official CCC Senior participants from schools in Canada are invited to the CCO at the University of Waterloo each spring", and that this invitation-only event "is also used to select Canada's teams for the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI)". So the path is CCC Senior, then the CCO by invitation, then the IOI team. CEMC's page sets out who counts as an official participant, so read its current rules.

faqs.question: Will this course get my child a distinction or a CCO invitation?
faqs.answer: No course can promise that, and we do not. Results depend on the student, the paper and the day. What the course gives is a full season of structured practice, timed mocks, honest reviews and an error log, so progress is visible month by month.

faqs.question: Does the CCC matter for university admission?
faqs.answer: It is a good experience, not a requirement. CEMC states that "Participation in the Canadian Computing Competition (CCC) is not required for admission to the Faculty of Mathematics at the University of Waterloo." We encourage students to write it for the problem solving it builds.

faqs.question: Does my child need coding experience?
faqs.answer: For the Junior track, a little: writing simple programs with variables, loops and conditions in Python or C++. For the Senior track, a student should be confident with lists or arrays, functions and basic sorting. The first-week diagnostic places each student, and our other coding courses are a good first step for complete beginners.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or 1-on-1. Junior and Senior students are taught in separate batches. Weekdays or weekends, flexible: choose your batch, or for a very personalised plan choose 1-on-1 at your convenience, weekend mornings or weekdays. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher works through a short original problem with your child, suggests the Junior or Senior track, and recommends group, mini batch or 1-on-1 classes. There is no obligation to enrol.
